source.title: Understanding Data Augmentation in Neural Machine Translation: Two Perspectives towards Generalization
source.authors: Guanlin Li; Le-Mao Liu; Guoping Huang; Cong-Hui Zhu; Tie-Jun Zhao

record.file_problem: Text appears complete; no evident garbling or truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests data-augmentation effects and training-set proxy measures in neural machine translation, a setting not covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports BLEU test results and two training-set measures for five augmentation methods across four translation tasks. BLEU is a task-specific test metric; input sensitivity and prediction margin are proxies, not direct measurements of the training–test error gap. No result directly tests V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study compares data augmentation methods in Transformer translation using BLEU, input sensitivity and prediction margin. None tests V1–V8. Input-embedding sensitivity is not magnitude-aware weight sharpness, and no training–test gap ranking is measured. Discussion and citations of generalization research do not make these experiments a test of the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that augmentation yields more consistent cross-task effects on input sensitivity and especially prediction margin than on BLEU, with benefits particularly for low-frequency words. They acknowledge disagreement between the two measures and suggest combining perspectives. They do not establish that either measure accurately ranks actual generalization gaps in these experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Studies data augmentation in Transformer NMT and measures BLEU, input sensitivity, and prediction margin; it does not use the original memorization, architecture, optimizer, batch, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Translation task and augmentation method change the results; BLEU rankings vary across tasks, and RAML/SO have negative margin changes while other methods have positive changes.

fits_no_version.finding: BLEU improvements depend on task and augmentation method. ST decreases Fr→En BLEU by 0.13; RAML and SO decrease En→De BLEU by 0.16 and 0.15. TA and BT improve BLEU in all four tasks. Cross-task ranking consistency is 0.62.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation does not uniformly improve held-out BLEU across NMT methods and translation tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Input sensitivity decreases in 17 of 20 comparisons. The three increases are RAML En→Fr (+0.003), BT En→Fr (+0.035) and BT En→De (+0.232). Cross-task ranking consistency is 0.72.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation often reduces training-set input-embedding sensitivity in NMT, with exceptions depending on task and method.

fits_no_version.finding: RAML and SO lower the measured prediction margin in all four tasks; ST, TA and BT raise it in all four. Cross-task ranking consistency is 0.98. These margins are computed from training subsamples, without validating their ranking against measured generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Augmentation methods have consistent directions of effect on the measured training-token prediction margin across these four translation tasks.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper reports proxy measures computed from training-set subsamples rather than the population risk–empirical risk gap. It notes that the measures do not show well consistency with each other; BLEU rankings vary across tasks. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: none; 60 rows retained (the maximum): BLEU changes from Table 1, sensitivity changes from Table 2, and margin changes from Table 3 for each of five methods and four translation tasks.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label versus random-label performance; the random-label comparison is discussed only as prior work.
Width sweeps, interpolation threshold and held-out error beyond the width required to fit.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity and initialization effects.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance and tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout addition or removal, training-set-size dependence and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its association with measured training–test gaps and its ranking against norm or margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equal-sized random removal and subsequent test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 baselines and changes match the supplied tables. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a listed effect; the numerical directions remain available under fits_no_version. The record incorrectly counts two positive sensitivity exceptions: there are three. No omitted result bears directly on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Network-width sweep and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Large versus small batch training and the effect of adapting the recipe.
Dropout interventions and their effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and its ranking of training–test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
